title: Frances Perkins: Influential and Unknown
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck profile Frances Perkins, the first woman to serve in a U.S. presidential cabinet as Secretary of Labor under FDR. They cover her Maine roots, Mount Holyoke and Columbia education, work with the Consumers League of New York and Florence Kelly, her reaction to the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Fire and subsequent New York fire-safety reforms, her work with Alfred E. Smith and FDR in New York, the Great Depression response, the Civilian Conservation Corps, the Wagner Act and Homestead speech, the Social Security Act and unemployment insurance, the Fair Labor Standards Act and child labor limits, the impeachment attempt over the Harry Bridges deportation case, and her use of Labor Department immigration powers to admit German Jewish refugees. The episode closes with a listener mail segment from Tawny about sewing face masks during COVID-19 and a Mister Rogers "look for the helper" quote.

segments.title: Book pre-order plug and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh promotes the Stuff You Should Know book pre-order, then the hosts introduce Frances Perkins as an undersung, influential American and discuss her Maine roots.

segments.title: Early life and education
segments.summary: The hosts describe Perkins's Yankee family roots in Maine, her conservative parents, her education at Mount Holyoke, Philadelphia work investigating fake employment agencies, and graduate study at Wharton and Columbia.

segments.title: Consumers League and the Triangle fire setup
segments.summary: Perkins works as executive secretary of the Consumers League of New York under Florence Kelly, focusing on labor conditions. The hosts introduce the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Fire, describing the factory's long hours, low pay, and locked doors.

segments.title: Triangle fire aftermath and New York fire codes
segments.summary: Perkins witnesses the fire and the deaths of victims, including a fire escape collapse. She pushes for fire codes in New York, including exit signs, occupancy limits, sprinklers, fire escapes, and unlocked doors, and is appointed to the New York Committee on Safety.

segments.title: Rise in New York politics under Smith and FDR
segments.summary: Perkins works with Alfred E. Smith, then with Franklin Roosevelt when he became governor. She becomes New York Industrial Commissioner and the first woman appointed to a state government position at that level, and she is the highest paid woman in an office in the US at the time.

segments.title: Secretary of Labor and New Deal programs
segments.summary: After the Depression hits, Perkins leads unemployment efforts, then becomes Secretary of Labor under FDR, the first woman in a cabinet. Labor unions initially resisted her. The hosts discuss the Civilian Conservation Corps, the Wagner Act, and her 1935 Homestead, Pennsylvania speech held at the post office.

segments.title: Social Security, Fair Labor Standards Act, and impeachment attempt
segments.summary: Perkins oversaw the cabinet committee that produced the Social Security Act, with the program unveiled to Congress soon after. She helped pass the Fair Labor Standards Act, minimum wage and maximum hours laws, and child labor limits. Congress tried to impeach her after she refused to deport Australian longshoreman Harry Bridges, whom she declined to deport.

segments.title: Later career, personal life, and refugee rescue
segments.summary: Perkins served until Truman's administration, published The Roosevelt I Knew, later served on the US Civil Service Commission, and taught at Cornell. The hosts discuss her care for her husband and daughter, her criticism of Hoover's economic claims, her note-taking on men, and her use of immigration quotas to admit German Jewish refugees before World War II.
